newsitem.title: MALI: Mali votes for president, opposition boycotts poll.
newsitem.headline: Mali votes for president, opposition boycotts poll.

text.p: Malians voted in presidential elections on Sunday with mainstream opposition parties boycotting the poll and President Alpha Oumar Konare promising to form a broad-based government if elected.

Witnesses said turnout was low, in contrast to a chaotic April 13 parliamentary election which prompted the impoverished West African nation's opposition to demand that this year's national elections be suspended and reorganised.
Konare, a historian elected in 1992 during Mali's widely praised democratic transition, faced one declared challenger -- businessman Hamadou Maribatrou Diaby. Both voted in the capital Bamako.
"After the election I will form a broad-based government open to all those of goodwill," Konare said afterwards.
Prime Minister Ibrahim Boubacar Keita told state radio that despite pre-poll opposition protests there were no reports of unrest. First results were expected on Sunday evening.
Polling stations offered ballot papers for eight other opposition candidates after the constitutional court ruled they had suspended but had not formally withdrawn their candidacy.
Opposition parties marched on Saturday urging people to boycott Sunday's polls and to demand that Konare stand down.

Voters flocked to polling stations on April 13 only to be thwarted by severe organisational problems. The constitutional court, at the request of the opposition, scrapped the results of that poll and ordered a fresh election.
It dismissed an opposition petition that Sunday's election should be postponed. The opposition had argued that a one-week delay announced by Konare could create confusion.
Witnesses said turnout half way through Sunday was low. The only exceptions were Kidal and Gao in the northeast, strongholds of Konare's ruling Alliance for Democracy in Mali ADEMA.
Polling was scheduled to end at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT).
Witnesses said differences between details on voter lists and voter cards caused problems, but fewer than on April 13.

Paramilitary gendarmes maintained a discreet watch on events after opposition protests in the run-up to polling. The government has closed schools and colleges after students threw stones and burned Konare campaign posters on Monday.
This year's polls, the second multi-party elections since independence from France in 1960, are widely seen as a key test of democracy. mali has five million eligible voters.
Political analysts in Bamako compare student demonstrations, power and water strikes with tension before the 1991 military overthrow of former one-party ruler General Moussa Traore.
Konare has steered the country on a course of economic liberalisation. He has won praise from the World Bank and the United States for his efforts.
